patient_note_history:
History

HPI: A 57-year-old male complains of one episode of painless hematuria yesterday morning with no association with fever, dysuria, abdominal or flank pain. He reports straining during urination, polyuria, nocturia, weak urinary stream, and dribbling. He has no history of earlier similar episodes or renal stones, no nausea, vomiting, diarrhea, or constipation, and no changes in appetite or weight loss.

ROS: Negative except as above.
Allergies: NKDA.
Medications: Allopurinol.
PMH: Gout.
PSH: I had an appendectomy when I was 23.
SH: He smokes 1 pack per day for 30 years, drinks 2 beers 2-3 times per week, has no history of illicit drug use, works as a painter, is heterosexual, has a partner, and uses condoms regularly.
FH: His father died from kidney disease at age 80.

exam_lines.source_text: The patient is in no acute distress.
Heart: regular rhythm and rate; S1/S2 within normal limits; no murmurs, rubs, or gallops.
Abdomen: soft, non-distended, non-tender, with active bowel sounds in all four quadrants; no hepatosplenomegaly. Mild tenderness at right costovertebral angle.

gold_additional_diagnosis:
• Prostate cancer: As mentioned above, this diagnosis is plausible but is hard to reconcile with the presence of CVA tenderness (it could postulate metastasis to a right posterior rib).

• Renal cell carcinoma: The classic triad is hematuria, flank pain, and a palpable mass. Constitutional symptoms may be prominent. The patient's other urinary symptoms may be due to coexisting BPH.

• Glomerulonephritis: The absence of hypertension or signs of volume overload (e.g., edema) argues against intrinsic renal disease. However, remember that IgA nephropathy is the most common acute glomerulonephritis and often presents with an episode of gross hematuria. Presentation is usually concurrent with URI, GI symptoms, or an Aulike illness.

• UTI: This can cause hematuria but is uncommon in males. The patient has no other symptoms to suggest an acute infection.

Examinee Tasks:

3. Explain your clinical impression and workup plan to the patient.
4. Write the patient note after leaving the room.

"They mentioned that the presence of blood in my urine is due to my age. Is that accurate?"

"No. Blood in the urine is infrequently considered normal.. We will need to run a few more tests to determine the cause of this finding."
